newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria looks for reform amid rows, doom forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Algeria looks for reform amid rows, doom forecasts.

text.p: Embroiled in political rows and boycotts and against forecasts of doom, Algeria's leadership and about 1,000 politicians are to gather on Saturday to chart a new future for the crisis-hit nation.

A much-vaunted "National Conference of Understanding" opens at the seaside complex of Club des Pins, 20 km (12 miles) from the overcrowded capital -- focus of much of the last five years' violence between Moslem fundamentalists and security forces.

The two main secular opposition parties are boycotting the conference, one charging that it will be a rubber-stamp for reforms already decided largely by President Liamine Zeroual, although the National Liberation Front (FLN), which ruled alone from independence from France in 1962 until 1988, will attend.

The once powerful Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), now outlawed, has not been invited. Earlier this week it said those taking part "would have to take entire responsibility for the consequences...of the aggravation of the crisis with its accompanying destruction, misery and poverty".

Algeria has been in crisis since January 1992 when authorities scrapped general elections in which FIS had taken a commanding lead. About 50,000 people have been killed and sabotage has cost the economy $2 billion.

"The conference...should offer various opportunities to resolve constitutionally questions on the country's future, while offering the possibility in Algeria and between Algerians the ways and means to end the crisis," the official Algerian news agency APS said on Wednesday.
The conference, after two years of tortuous talks, is to look at three main recommended reforms:
-- Proportional representation instead of first-past-the-post election system which officials believe gave the FIS victory in the elections cancelled in 1992;
-- A ban on the use of religion as a political weapon, although existing parties founded on religion, like the legal Hamas, will have a year to change their focus and conform;
-- Confirmation that Islam is the state religion in this North African country of 29 million people.
Zeroual, 55, who has nurtured the conference for two years, has promised a referendum afterwards to ratify the reforms. He also promises general elections early in 1997.
The two main secular opposition parties boycotting the conference are the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) and the Rally for Democracy and Culture (RCD).
The FFS, which came second in the aborted general election, walked out of preparatory talks saying the whole thing was a plot by Zeroual to consecrate "a constitutional dictatorship".
The RCD, rival of the FFS in the mainly Berber northeast, said it would boycott the meeting because the authorities had backtracked on proposals like recognising Tamazigh, the Berber language.

The main legal Islamic party, Hamas, whose leader Mahfoud Nahnah won 2.9 million votes in last November's presidential election which confirmed the appointed Zeroual in power, has grudgingly agreed to attend.
